sentences.text: Shonisaurus popularis was a massive creature with a skull measuring about 2.75 meters long and a total body length between 13.5 and 15 meters.
This animal featured a long snout and flippers that were much longer and narrower than those seen in other ichthyosaurs.
Studies since the early 1990s reveal that Shonisaurus had a much more slender body than traditionally thought, though it remained relatively deep compared to related marine reptiles.
The large tail fin typically reconstructed for Shonisaurus was likely not as developed as that of later ichthyosaur species, which possessed a tail profile more similar to sharks.
Recent findings indicate that Shonisaurus possessed teeth in all stages of growth, contrary to earlier reports that claimed socketed teeth existed only in juveniles.
Scientists have uncovered at least 37 incomplete fossils of Shonisaurus popularis within the Luning Formation of Nevada.
Due to its significance, Shonisaurus popularis was officially adopted as the state fossil of Nevada in 1984.
Fossils of Shonisaurus were first discovered in a large deposit in Nevada in 1920.
The name Shonisaurus means "lizard from the Shoshone Mountains" and refers to the geological formation where the fossils were found.
The genus Shonisaurus was formally named by Charles Camp in 1976.
A second species, Shonisaurus sikanniensis, was named in 2004 from fossils found in the Pardonet Formation of British Columbia.
An ichthyosaur found in the Himalayas called Himalayasaurus might actually be the same animal as Shonisaurus.
Shonisaurus is classified within the family Shastasauridae.
The genus authority for Shonisaurus is recorded as Camp, 1976.
Shonisaurus lived from the Carnian to the Rhaetian stages, between 233.6 and 201.4 million years ago.
A 2011 study suggested that Shonisaurus sikanniensis might actually be a species of Shastasaurus rather than Shonisaurus.
Later studies have supported both hypotheses regarding the classification of Shonisaurus sikanniensis, with some authors placing it in Shonisaurus and others in Shastasaurus.
It is debated whether Shonisaurus possessed a dorsal fin, as there is no solid evidence that it or other shastasaurids had this feature.
